description: Registry of scoured early cinema and chronophotography works with verified public domain provenance.

sources.title: The Horse in Motion — Sallie Gardner at a Gallop
sources.creator: Eadweard Muybridge
sources.summary: Leland Stanford's mare Sallie Gardner galloping at Palo Alto track, proving all four hooves leave the ground simultaneously.
sources.description: Captured in June 1878 at the Palo Alto Stock Farm using a battery of 24 cameras with electro-magnetic shutter releases triggered by tripwires. Published in 1881 as 'The Attitudes of Animals in Motion'. One of the foundational achievements in the history of high-speed photography and moving images.
sources.archive: Library of Congress / Stanford University Archives
sources.credit: Eadweard Muybridge, 1878. The Horse in Motion: Sallie Gardner. Palo Alto Stock Farm / Library of Congress. Public domain.

sources.title: Athletes Boxing — Animal Locomotion (Plate 333)
sources.creator: Eadweard Muybridge
sources.summary: Two athletes boxing and sparring, captured in sequential high-speed chronophotography for the University of Pennsylvania.
sources.description: Plate 333 from Eadweard Muybridge's 1887 landmark portfolio 'Animal Locomotion: An Electro-Photographic Investigation of Consecutive Phases of Animal Movements' (University of Pennsylvania). Demonstrates rapid footwork, defensive guards, and jab exchanges, ideal for dual-person pose estimation.
sources.archive: University of Pennsylvania / Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division
sources.credit: Eadweard Muybridge, 1887. Athletes Boxing (Animal Locomotion, Plate 333). University of Pennsylvania. Public domain.

sources.title: Athletes Fencing — Animal Locomotion (Plate 348)
sources.creator: Eadweard Muybridge
sources.summary: Two athletes fencing with foils, performing lunges, parries, and thrusts in sequential multi-camera photography.
sources.description: Plate 348 from Eadweard Muybridge's 1887 'Animal Locomotion' portfolio. Features two fencers in white and dark fencing kit performing lunges and parries, showing the biomechanics of fencing with extreme clarity.
sources.archive: University of Pennsylvania / Library of Congress
sources.credit: Eadweard Muybridge, 1887. Athletes Fencing (Animal Locomotion, Plate 348). University of Pennsylvania. Public domain.

sources.title: Chronophotographie géométrique — Homme marchant en combinaison noire
sources.creator: Étienne-Jules Marey
sources.summary: Étienne-Jules Marey's landmark geometrical chronophotography of a man walking in a black suit with white line markers — the historic foundation of optical motion capture.
sources.description: Recorded in 1883 at the Station Physiologique in Paris. Marey dressed his subject in a black velvet bodysuit with bright white reflective stripes along the limbs and joints, exposing the plate intermittently with a rotating slotted disc. This breakthrough reduced human gait to pure kinetic geometry and directly inspired 20th-century motion capture and pose estimation.
sources.archive: Collège de France / Cinémathèque française / Société française de photographie
sources.credit: Étienne-Jules Marey, 1883. Chronophotographie géométrique (Homme marchant). Station Physiologique, Paris / Collège de France. Public domain.

sources.title: Saut de haies par l'athlète américain Alvin Kraenzlein
sources.creator: Étienne-Jules Marey
sources.summary: Olympic champion Alvin Kraenzlein demonstrating his revolutionary straight-leg hurdling technique at the 1900 Paris Exposition.
sources.description: Recorded on continuous moving celluloid film by Étienne-Jules Marey at the Station Physiologique de Paris during the 1900 Summer Olympic Games. Alvin Kraenzlein was the four-time gold medalist who invented the modern hurdling technique of clearing the hurdle with a straight front leg. Excellent for high-speed body tracking.
sources.archive: Collège de France / Cinémathèque française / Archives françaises du film (CNC)
sources.commons_file: File:Saut de haie par l'americain Alvin Kraenzlein (1900).webm
sources.credit: Étienne-Jules Marey, 1900. Saut de haie par Alvin Kraenzlein. Station Physiologique de Paris / Collège de France. Public domain.

sources.title: The Boxing Cats (Prof. Welton's)
sources.creator: William K.L. Dickson
sources.summary: Henry Welton's trained domestic cats sparring with miniature boxing gloves in a miniature ring at Thomas Edison's Black Maria studio.
sources.description: Filmed in July 1894 at Edison's Black Maria studio in West Orange, New Jersey by William K.L. Dickson and William Heise. Deposited for copyright protection as a paper print in the Library of Congress. One of the earliest animal motion pictures in cinema history and an iconic early internet favorite.
sources.archive: Library of Congress Motion Picture, Broadcasting and Recorded Sound Division
sources.credit: William K.L. Dickson and William Heise (Edison Kinetoscope), 1894. The Boxing Cats (Prof. Welton's). Library of Congress Paper Print Collection. Public domain.

sources.title: L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat
sources.creator: Louis Lumière
sources.summary: A steam locomotive pulling passenger cars into the station of La Ciotat as travelers disembark along the platform.
sources.description: Filmed in late 1895 with the Cinématographe by Louis and Auguste Lumière. Famous for its diagonal composition from upper-right to lower-left foreground, introducing visual depth and perspective to moving picture audiences.
sources.archive: Institut Lumière (Lyon) / Centre national du cinéma et de l'image animée (CNC)
sources.commons_file: File:Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat (The Lumière Brothers, 1895).webm
sources.credit: Louis Lumière, 1895. L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat (Vue n° 653). Institut Lumière / CNC. Public domain.

sources.title: L'Homme à la tête de caoutchouc (The Man with the Rubber Head)
sources.creator: Georges Méliès
sources.summary: Georges Méliès places his living head on a laboratory table and uses a bellows to inflate it until it fills the room and bursts.
sources.description: Produced by Georges Méliès at the Star Film studio in Montreuil (Star Film catalog no. 361–362). Méliès accomplished the camera scale effect by placing himself on a wheeled trolley moving toward the stationary camera against a black velvet background, double-exposed onto the chemist's laboratory set. A foundational milestone in visual special effects, ideal for facial tracking and generative deformation.
sources.archive: Cinémathèque française / Library of Congress Paper Print Collection
sources.commons_file: File:L'homme à la tête en caoutchouc (1901).webm
sources.credit: Georges Méliès, 1901. L'Homme à la tête de caoutchouc (Star Film no. 361–362). Cinémathèque française / Library of Congress. Public domain.

sources.title: Das boxende Känguruh (The Boxing Kangaroo)
sources.creator: Max Skladanowsky
sources.summary: A boxing kangaroo sparring against circus artist Delaware, projected with the Bioscop at the Berlin Wintergarten in November 1895.
sources.description: Recorded in 1895 by Max and Emil Skladanowsky with the Bioscop dual-projector system. Shown at the Berlin Wintergarten theatre starting on 1 November 1895, making the Skladanowsky brothers among the very first commercial moving picture exhibitors in Europe.
sources.credit: Max Skladanowsky, 1895. Das boxende Känguruh (Bioscop). Bundesarchiv / Deutsches Filmmuseum. Public domain.
